title: Enhancing characteristics: comparability, consistency, verifiability, timeliness, understandability, and the cost constraint
summary: How comparability differs from consistency and uniformity, the other enhancing characteristics, how they are applied, and why cost limits reporting.

chunks.heading: Comparability: the goal
chunks.explanation_md:
Users' decisions are about **choosing between alternatives**: sell or hold an investment, invest in one entity or another. So information is more useful if it can be **compared** with similar information about **other entities** and with similar information about **the same entity for another period or date**.

**Comparability** is the characteristic that lets users **identify and understand similarities in, and differences among, items.** Unlike the other characteristics it does **not relate to a single item**: a comparison needs **at least two items**.

Some comparability comes automatically from meeting the fundamental characteristics. A faithful representation of a relevant phenomenon should naturally be somewhat comparable with a faithful representation of a similar phenomenon by another entity.

A single economic phenomenon can be faithfully represented in more than one way, but **allowing alternative accounting methods for the same phenomenon reduces comparability**.

key_terms.meaning: The characteristic that enables users to identify and understand similarities in, and differences among, items; it needs at least two items.

chunks.exam_line: Comparability lets users identify similarities and differences between entities and between periods of the same entity. It needs at least two items. Alternative methods for the same item reduce it.

chunks.heading: Consistency helps comparability, and comparability is not uniformity
chunks.explanation_md:
**Consistency is related to comparability but is not the same thing.** Consistency means using the **same methods for the same items**, either **from period to period within one entity** or **in a single period across entities**. The slide's key line: **comparability is the goal; consistency helps to achieve that goal.**

**Comparability is not uniformity.** For information to be comparable, **like things must look alike and different things must look different**. Making unlike things look alike does not improve comparability, any more than making like things look different does.

**Trade-offs.** The enhancing characteristics should be maximised as far as possible, but sometimes one has to be reduced to maximise another. Example: a **temporary reduction in comparability** from applying a new Standard prospectively may be worthwhile to improve relevance or faithful representation in the longer term. **Appropriate disclosures may partly make up** for non-comparability.

chunks.heading: Verifiability
chunks.explanation_md:
**Verifiability** helps assure users that information **faithfully represents** what it claims to. It means that **different knowledgeable and independent observers could reach consensus**, though not necessarily complete agreement, that a depiction is a faithful representation.

A quantified figure need not be a single point estimate to be verifiable. A **range of possible amounts and their probabilities** can be verified too.

**Direct verification:** checking an amount by direct observation, for example **counting cash**.

**Indirect verification:** checking the **inputs** to a model or formula and **recalculating the outputs** with the same method. Example from the slide: verify the carrying amount of **inventory** by checking the **quantities and costs** and recalculating ending inventory using the same cost flow assumption, for example **first-in, first-out**.

Some explanations and **forward-looking information** may not be verifiable until a future period, if ever. To help users decide whether to use it, the entity should normally **disclose the underlying assumptions, the methods of compiling it and other supporting factors**.

key_terms.meaning: Different knowledgeable and independent observers could reach consensus that a depiction is a faithful representation.

chunks.exam_line: Verification can be direct (count cash) or indirect (check inputs and recalculate outputs, such as inventory with the same cost flow assumption). Forward-looking information needs disclosure of assumptions and methods.

chunks.heading: Timeliness and understandability
chunks.explanation_md:
**Timeliness:** having information available to decision-makers **in time to be capable of influencing their decisions**. In general, **the older the information, the less useful it is**. Some information stays timely long after the period ends, because some users need it to identify and assess **trends**.

**Understandability:** **classifying, characterising and presenting information clearly and concisely** makes it understandable.

- Some phenomena are **inherently complex** and cannot be made easy. Leaving them out would make reports easier to read but **incomplete and possibly misleading**.
- Reports are prepared for users with a **reasonable knowledge of business and economic activities** who review and analyse the information **diligently**. At times even well-informed users may need an **adviser** for complex phenomena.
chunks.exam_line: Timeliness: information available in time to influence decisions; older information is generally less useful. Understandability: clear and concise classification and presentation, without omitting complex but necessary items.

chunks.heading: Applying the enhancing characteristics
chunks.explanation_md:
- Enhancing characteristics should be **maximised as far as possible**. But they **cannot make information useful** if it is irrelevant or not a faithful representation.
- They may also help choose between **two ways of depicting a phenomenon** when both are equally relevant and equally faithful.
- Applying them is an **iterative process with no prescribed order**.
- Sometimes one has to be **diminished to maximise another**. Example: a temporary reduction in comparability from applying a new Standard prospectively.
- **Appropriate disclosures** may partly compensate for non-comparability.

So the fundamental characteristics come first; the enhancing ones add to information that already passes that test.
chunks.exam_line: Enhancing characteristics add to relevant, faithful information but cannot rescue irrelevant or unfaithful information; applying them is iterative with no prescribed order.

chunks.heading: The cost constraint
chunks.explanation_md:
**Cost is a pervasive constraint** on reporting. The costs must be **justified by the benefits** of reporting the information.

**Costs.** Providers do most of the work of **collecting, processing, verifying and disseminating** information, but **users bear those costs ultimately** through reduced returns. Users also bear costs of **analysing and interpreting**. If needed information is not provided, users pay extra to **obtain it elsewhere or estimate it**.

**Benefits.** Reporting relevant, faithfully represented information helps users decide **with more confidence**, which means **more efficient capital markets** and a **lower cost of capital** for the economy, and better decisions for individual investors and creditors. Still, general purpose reports cannot give every user all the information they find relevant.

**How the Board applies it.** The Board checks whether the benefits are likely to justify the costs. It asks providers, users, auditors, academics and others, using **quantitative and qualitative** information. Because assessments are subjective, it considers costs and benefits for **financial reporting generally**, not just individual entities. That does not mean the same requirements for all: **size, how capital is raised (publicly or privately), users' needs** and other factors can justify differences.

key_terms.meaning: The requirement that the costs of reporting information be justified by its benefits.

chunks.exam_line: Cost is a pervasive constraint: the benefits of information must justify the costs for providers and users. The Board assesses costs and benefits for reporting generally; differences between entities can be appropriate.

questions.stem: Discuss the enhancing qualitative characteristics of useful financial information, with particular reference to comparability and consistency.
questions.model_answer_md:
Enhancing characteristics (**comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability**) make information that is already relevant and faithfully represented more useful.

**Comparability.** Users choose between alternatives, so information is more useful if it can be compared with information about other entities and with the same entity's information for another period. Comparability helps users identify similarities and differences. It needs at least two items. It is **not uniformity**: like things must look alike and different things different. Allowing alternative methods for the same phenomenon reduces it.

**Consistency** means using the same methods for the same items, over periods or across entities. Comparability is the goal and consistency helps achieve it.

**Verifiability.** Independent, knowledgeable observers could reach consensus that a depiction is faithful. It can be direct (counting cash) or indirect (checking inputs and recalculating, for example inventory with a given cost flow assumption).

**Timeliness.** Information must be available in time to influence decisions; older information is generally less useful.

**Understandability.** Clear, concise classification and presentation; complex phenomena should not be excluded.

**Applying them.** They should be maximised but cannot make irrelevant information useful. Application is iterative; sometimes one is reduced to improve another, for example a temporary fall in comparability when a new Standard is applied prospectively, with disclosures to compensate.

Cost limits all of them.

questions.stem: A company changes its inventory cost flow method every year. Using the Conceptual Framework's ideas, explain the effect on comparability and what the Framework says about such trade-offs.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Effect on comparability.** Comparability lets users compare an entity with others and with itself over time. **Consistency**, the same methods for the same items from period to period, helps to achieve it. If the method changes every year, the same item is reported differently and users cannot compare periods. Allowing alternative methods for the same phenomenon diminishes comparability.

**Verifiability.** Inventory can be verified indirectly by checking quantities and costs and recalculating ending inventory with the same cost flow assumption, so the method matters for checking too.

**Trade-offs.** The Framework accepts that one enhancing characteristic may sometimes be reduced to improve another. For example, a **temporary reduction in comparability** when a new Standard is applied prospectively may be worthwhile for better relevance or faithful representation in the longer term, and **appropriate disclosures** may partly compensate.

So a change should be justified by better information and be disclosed; changing without reason weakens comparability.

Inventory verification uses the same cost flow assumption
